drills.q: Walk through the five stages of the browser rendering pipeline from raw HTML/CSS to pixels on screen.
drills.a: Parse HTML into DOM and CSS into CSSOM (both incremental; CSS is render-blocking). Combine into a render tree of visible nodes with computed style. Layout computes geometry (x/y/width/height) for every box. Paint rasterizes pixel content per layer. Composite (on a separate compositor thread) assembles layers into the final frame, applying transform/opacity as cheap GPU operations.

drills.q: Explain the mechanism (not just the rule) for why transform is cheaper to animate than top/left.
drills.a: top/left are geometry properties -- changing them invalidates layout, which must run on the main thread, followed by paint, followed by composite, contending with all other main-thread work for the frame budget. transform on an already-promoted GPU layer skips layout and paint entirely; the compositor thread reapplies a matrix transform to the already-rasterized texture, running independent of the main thread.

drills.q: Contrast display:none and visibility:hidden in terms of render tree membership and layout cost.
drills.a: display:none removes the element from the render tree entirely: no layout, no paint, zero cost, no occupied space. visibility:hidden keeps it in the render tree, fully laid out (occupies space, affects sibling positions) but skips painting it -- cheaper to toggle when layout stability of surrounding content matters.

drills.q: What is forced synchronous layout / layout thrashing, give a code example of the bug, and the fix.
drills.a: Reading a geometry property (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, getComputedStyle) immediately after a style write forces the browser to synchronously flush layout to answer correctly. Looping write-then-read per element (el.style.width = el.offsetWidth + 10 + 'px') turns one lazy layout pass into N synchronous ones. Fix: batch all reads first, then apply all writes.

drills.q: A DevTools Performance trace shows large purple bars on every frame during a scroll interaction. Diagnose and confirm.
drills.a: Purple = Layout/Recalculate Style; hypothesis is a scroll handler or scroll-triggered effect is changing a geometry property (e.g. animating top for a parallax effect) every frame. Confirm by clicking into a purple bar to see the triggering call stack, and cross-check with paint flashing / Layout Shift Regions in the Rendering tab.

drills.q: What does will-change actually do, what does it cost, and why is applying it broadly a mistake?
drills.a: It promotes the element to its own GPU-backed compositing layer in advance, avoiding a layer-creation cost on the animation's first frame. Cost: each layer consumes GPU memory (~width*height*4 bytes texture) plus compositing overhead. Applying it to many elements or leaving it on permanently causes 'layer explosion,' which measurably degrades performance on GPU/memory-constrained devices -- it should be toggled on right before an animation and off (will-change:auto) after.

drills.q: Why does a render-blocking stylesheet in <head> delay First Contentful Paint even when the HTML itself arrives instantly?
drills.a: The browser can't safely paint until the CSSOM is complete, because any rule anywhere in an unparsed stylesheet could apply to already-parsed DOM nodes -- painting early risks showing incorrectly styled content that must then be redone. Fix: inline critical above-the-fold CSS, defer the rest, mark scripts defer/async so they don't also block parsing.

drills.q: Explain the difference between defer and async on a <script> tag and why an unmarked script blocks parsing at all.
drills.a: An unmarked synchronous script can call document.write() and mutate the DOM being parsed, so the parser halts until it downloads and executes. defer downloads in parallel with parsing but executes after parsing completes, in document order relative to other deferred scripts. async downloads in parallel and executes as soon as ready, with no ordering guarantee relative to parsing or other scripts.

drills.q: What is the frame budget at 60Hz vs 120Hz, and why is requestAnimationFrame correct where setTimeout is not?
drills.a: 16.7ms at 60Hz, 8.3ms at 120Hz (1000/refresh rate). requestAnimationFrame schedules its callback synced to the actual next paint at whatever the display's real refresh rate is, adapting automatically. setTimeout has no relationship to the paint cycle at all and will drift or misfire relative to the true frame cadence, especially on non-60Hz displays.

drills.q: A drag-to-reorder list needs siblings to visibly make room as an item is dragged. Can this be done compositor-only, and what's the real technique?
drills.a: Not purely -- siblings' actual flow position is genuinely changing, which is a layout-affecting change. The realistic approach is FLIP (First-Last-Invert-Play): commit the real layout change once/synchronously, then animate only the visual delta between old and new position via transform on each affected element -- the dragged item itself can move via pure transform following the pointer the whole time.

drills.q: Why can a large box-shadow be a measurable performance problem, and what CSS tool isolates it without the memory cost of will-change?
drills.a: Rasterizing a shadow's blur/spread is more expensive than a flat fill, and if the element shares a paint-invalidation region with something that repaints often, the expensive shadow gets re-rasterized far more than its own visual state changes. contain:paint (or contain:content) scopes paint invalidation to the element's own subtree without necessarily promoting a full GPU layer the way will-change does -- a lighter-weight fix for this specific problem.

drills.q: Is layout cost a fixed O(1) operation per DOM change? Explain what actually determines its cost, and how contain:layout changes that.
drills.a: No fixed constant -- cost depends on how far the geometry change propagates: a leaf absolutely-positioned node can be nearly free, while an early flow-participating element's height change can force re-layout of every subsequent sibling and a content-sized parent, proportional to the affected subtree. contain:layout gives the engine a real guarantee that an element's internal layout can't affect anything outside its box (and vice versa), letting it scope invalidation to just that subtree rather than relying on heuristics -- valuable for large lists/grids of independently-changing items.
